title: Topera
summary: Creative Navy produced a three-sprint concept design for Topera, a planned platform for industrial development projects that span multiple organisations. The documented work centred on deriving an information architecture from DIN 69901 and ProSTEP iViP / VDA standards, setting scope by synchronisation depth, and designing concept surfaces for portfolio overview, work breakdown structure, scheduling and project definition. The evidence base is intentionally limited: no research, testing, build, deployment or measured outcome is claimed.
keyFacts: Topera is a planned cross-organisational project management platform, not a built or deployed product.
The engagement lasted three one-week sprints and involved a UX designer, UI designer, product designer and project manager.
Creative Navy scoped a full design of the platform at twenty-four one-week sprints before the engagement; the client commissioned three as a concept design.
The client supplied nine standards documents: DIN 69901 parts 1 to 5, PSI 1-1, PSI 1-2, PSI 10 / VDA 4959 and PSI 25.
Creative Navy produced three written documents: an information architecture mapping, a design requirements document and a revised design specification.
The concept covered the Project Overview Dashboard, Work Breakdown Structure view, Schedule & Milestones view and Project Definition start-up flow.
The design output included twenty-four unique screens, a style guide and four complete UI style directions.

DIN 69901-2 defines fifty-nine project management processes, including fourteen Mindeststandard processes; all fourteen appeared in Creative Navy's architecture mapping and design requirements documents.
No user research, usability testing, UX audit, competitor benchmarking, build or development handover took place.
The only outcome-adjacent evidence is client-reported: Topera's team was pleased with the concept design and took it to show stakeholders.

bodySections.heading: Topera as a Concept Design for Cross-Organisational Project Management
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Topera is a planned cross-organisational project management platform. It was conceived for industrial development projects that span more than one organisation, where a coordinating organisation and partner organisations each hold part of the same project plan and need to keep those parts synchronised without merging their internal systems.

Creative Navy scoped a full design of the platform at twenty-four one-week sprints and put that position to the client before the engagement began. The client commissioned three one-week sprints as a concept design. The twenty-four-sprint figure is Creative Navy's professional estimate of the full design scope, not a measured comparison between two pieces of work.

The central design judgement was therefore about the purpose of the deliverable. The Topera engagement was not a compressed full product design. It was a concept design intended to make the product architecture, scope boundary and interface direction legible enough for decision-making.

bodySections.heading: Standards Corpus Supplied for the Topera Concept Design
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The client supplied the standards corpus for the Topera concept design. The nine documents were DIN 69901 parts 1 to 5, the ProSTEP iViP CPM Reference Model (PSI 1-1), the ProSTEP iViP CPM Data Exchange Model (PSI 1-2), the ProSTEP iViP / VDA schedule management recommendation (PSI 10 / VDA 4959), and the ProSTEP iViP PSMS recommendation (PSI 25).

DIN 69901 parts 1 to 5 are German standards documents covering fundamentals, processes and process model, methods, data and data model, and terminology. The working vocabulary in the Topera specification was therefore bilingual: German standard terms such as Vorhaben, Projektstrukturplan, Arbeitspaket, Vorgang, Meilenstein, Netzplantechnik, Terminmanagement, Soll-Ist-Vergleich and Pufferzeit were mapped to English interface terms.

The standards were process models, data models and cross-company coordination recommendations. They did not define an interface. Creative Navy's work was to synthesise those standards into an information architecture, screen structure and concept-level interaction model. The engagement did not certify Topera to any standard, audit Topera against any standard, or establish conformance with DIN, ProSTEP iViP or VDA recommendations.

bodySections.heading: Creative Navy Derived a Two-Axis Architecture from DIN 69901 and PSI 25
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method was applied in the Topera engagement as domain learning from a normative corpus rather than from user research. The design work started from published standards supplied by the client and converted them into an information architecture for a system that did not yet exist.

The central artefact was a matrix with two axes. The horizontal time axis carried the five DIN 69901-2 project management phases: Initialisation, Definition, Planning, Execution and Monitoring, and Closure. The vertical knowledge axis carried eleven management domains: project structure, schedule and milestones, communication and reporting, cost and budget, human resources, resources, quality, risk, contract, deliverables, and change management.

Every cell of the matrix was populated with three elements: the DIN 69901-2 processes active in that phase, the DIN 69901-4 data model entities that carry the information, and the PSI 25 synchronisation activity that propagates the information to partners. This made the derivation traceable in both directions: from a standard element to the screen that realised it, and from a screen back to the standard element that justified it.

DIN 69901-2 defines fifty-nine project management processes across five phases and eleven process groups. Fourteen are designated Mindeststandard, the minimum set every project must run. All fourteen Mindeststandard process codes appeared in Creative Navy's architecture mapping and design requirements documents: D.8.3, D.11.1, P.1.2, P.7.1, P.8.1, P.8.2, P.9.1, S.1.2, S.2.1, S.3.2, S.7.1, S.8.1, S.11.1 and A.6.1. This supports a narrow claim: the derivation covered the standard's named minimum set. It does not establish build readiness, design adequacy or standards conformance.

bodySections.heading: Work Breakdown Structure Design Followed DIN 69901-4's Polymorphic Initiative Entity
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
DIN 69901-4 uses Vorhaben, or initiative, as a central polymorphic entity. The same entity type represents a project, work package, activity and milestone, distinguished by a type attribute and nested through a sub-initiative relationship that forms the work breakdown hierarchy.

Creative Navy's Topera concept used that modelling decision to design the Work Breakdown Structure view as one structural surface rather than separate surfaces for each item type. The view was designed as a tree carrying project, work package, task and subtask items, with milestones as a further typed item. Expandability was designed to appear only where children exist.

A right-hand detail panel was designed to carry the selected item while preserving the structural tree. The panel was organised into tabs for time, finance, quality, delivery, communication and files. Plan, actual and forecast dates were kept structurally separate, with a plan block and an actual block, and the actual block separately editable and explicitly saved.

The Work Breakdown Structure view was designed from two legitimate entry points: one reached from Projects navigation and one reached from Domains navigation. These were not recorded as client-selected alternatives. They were designed as co-equal routes into the same structure.

bodySections.heading: Topera's MVP Scope Was Specified by Synchronisation Depth
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method used progressive specification in the Topera engagement by setting the MVP boundary against PSI 25 synchronisation levels. The design did not define scope only as a list of features. It defined scope in terms of how deeply two companies would synchronise project schedule information.

PSI 25 defines synchronisation levels from SL1.1 through SL3.x. The ladder begins with project master data, dependencies and work packages at project or partner level; rises through individual milestones, activities with dependencies, and deliverable references; and reaches complete network plans with sub-projects and multiple partners. Partners at different levels can still work together.

Creative Navy specified SL1.1 and SL1.2 as required, SL2.1 and SL2.2 as target, SL2.3 as stretch, and SL3.x as post-MVP. The same ladder was applied to CPM collaboration classes, with CC1 to CC3 in scope and CC4 deferred. This made the MVP boundary externally legible because the boundary was tied to a published synchronisation model rather than an internal feature taxonomy.

The data model coverage was also tiered. The DIN 69901-4 data model areas were designated as core, MVP-domain or simplified for the MVP. At the same time, the architecture was required to remain complete even where the MVP was not: non-implemented areas still had to appear as future extension points.

bodySections.heading: The Partner Organisation Boundary Was Treated as a Designed Object
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method used constraint respecting in the Topera concept by treating the partner organisation boundary as a design constraint rather than only as a permissions rule. Internal users were specified to see full project depth. External partners were specified as asynchronous participants, with three to four structural levels exposed and no direct edit permissions.

The same project objects therefore had two legitimate views at different resolutions. The partner-facing view was shallower by design, not because the underlying project structure was different.

The handover model made the boundary more explicit. One party was specified to create an initiative and assign it to another party with constraint attributes attached: maximum duration, maximum effort and maximum cost. The receiving party would see the assigned sub-initiative and its constraints, then decompose further within them. The concept was specified to warn, but not prevent, when decomposition passed four levels. The final structure was specified as a stitched tree with aggregated values.

Two forms of progress reporting were also specified as valid inputs. A domain system returning a time series of actual effort and a domain system returning discrete milestone-style dates were both accepted, rather than one being normalised into the other.

bodySections.heading: Schedule and Milestone Design Followed Network Planning Requirements
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Schedule & Milestones view was designed around network planning rather than only around a Gantt bar chart. Dependencies were typed as finish-to-start, start-to-start, finish-to-finish and start-to-finish, with lead and lag. The critical path was designed as a distinct display mode. Float was designed as a displayable quantity, with free float and total float distinguished. Baseline comparison was designed as an overlay.

DIN 69900 governs Netzplantechnik, or network planning technique. The specification cited requirements from DIN 69900 that are directly about interface behaviour, including separate scalability of the horizontal time axis in usual units of time and maintenance of scheduled dates by drag and drop in graphical display forms such as the Gantt chart.

Direct manipulation of the schedule was therefore designed as a requirement rather than a convenience feature. The concept specified drag to reschedule, with dependent task recalculation, conflict highlighting and critical-path recomputation following from it. The Gantt information columns were also designed as configurable, so the same timeline could carry different supporting columns such as status, owner, dates, progress, priority or responsible organisation.

bodySections.heading: Concept Surfaces Covered Portfolio Triage, Project Definition, Work Structure and Schedule Control
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy-recorded engagement evidence shows that the Topera concept design covered four main surfaces: the Project Overview Dashboard, the Work Breakdown Structure view, the Schedule & Milestones view, and the Project Definition start-up flow. Supporting flows included data import with validation and duplicate handling, template-library import, bulk item creation, filtering and view configuration.

The Project Overview Dashboard was designed as a portfolio-level triage surface. It paired a statistical summary group with a dense project table carrying status, completion, milestone counts, warnings, team, phase and last update. Warning indicators were designed to be interrogable in place through tooltips naming the specific condition. Completed projects could be hidden through an explicit toggle.

The Project Definition start-up surface was designed as a single long working page rather than as a wizard. A left navigation listed definition areas with per-area completion state, a central working column carried the work, and a right panel carried settings, recommendations and contextual validation. The areas corresponded to DIN 69901-2 processes in the DIN 69901-2 Definition phase. Completion was designed to be tracked persistently, and the phase transition into Planning was designed as an explicit clearance gate with incomplete and blocked items identified.

The data import flow was designed around failure as well as success. File validation included per-row error reporting that named the field and the fault. Duplicate detection was specified as a separate step listing colliding identifiers and offering an explicit choice between importing as new data and importing to overwrite. These were designed screens, not only transient error messages.

bodySections.heading: Option Space Mapping Was Visible in the Concept Boards
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method used option space mapping in the Topera engagement at the architecture and interface-pattern level. The evidence is limited to what the boards show was produced. There is no record of client choices between alternatives, no written feedback rounds and no transcript of working sessions.

The boards show two structural versions of the Project Overview Dashboard, differing in how the summary band carried information. The boards also show four filter patterns for the same table: an inline pattern, a cascading menu pattern, a full right-hand filter panel with grouped and collapsible criteria including saved filters, and a chip-based pattern where each applied filter became a removable token.

Four complete UI style directions were produced for the same screen, differing in typography, accent colour and surface treatment and spanning light and dark treatments. Two right-panel treatments were produced for the Project Definition surface, along with a collapsed-areas treatment of the same page. Two navigation treatments were produced for the Work Breakdown Structure: a full domain panel and a collapsed icon rail.

The hardest Work Breakdown Structure board reached at least a fourth documented version. This is an iteration count, not a user-validated result. It supports the statement that alternatives and iterations were produced; it does not support a claim about what the client selected, preferred or rejected.

bodySections.heading: Three One-Week Sprints Produced a Concept Artefact, Not a Build-Ready System
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy-recorded engagement evidence states that the Topera engagement produced three written documents: an information architecture mapping of DIN project management processes, a design requirements document specifying the MVP scope module by module against the standards, and a revised design specification covering the designed screens in detail. All three were Creative Navy's synthesis of the standards supplied by the client.

The concept output included twenty-four unique screens. This is the count of distinct screens, not a count of frames, states or visual variants. The state and variant designs, the four UI style directions and the style guide sit on top of that number and are not counted in it.

A style guide was produced covering colour, typography, corner radius, layout and spacing, icons, and a documented set of action components including buttons, text fields, dropdowns, selection controls, tables, tabs, badges, modals, tooltips, notifications and progress indicators. Component pages documented states rather than a single appearance. No style guide page count or component count is established.

The concept also specified states across the main surfaces, including hover, selected, empty, expanded, collapsed, read-only, error and validation-failure states. Read-only state was designed to be shown on the item through a lock indicator, with explanation and route to the owner available from it. Dependent sections were designed to declare blockers rather than fail silently.

bodySections.heading: Critical Systems Design Phases Claimable for Topera Are Limited
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method is only partially claimable in the Topera engagement. The documented work supports Sandbox Experiments and Concept Convergence with qualifications. It does not support Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration or Implementation Partnership.

Sandbox Experiments is supported as option space mapping at the architecture level, visible in the produced alternatives and documented iterations. The qualification is important: the engagement did not include the embedded research that Sandbox Experiments normally carries. There were no interviews, observations, user workshops or contact with project managers, programme managers or partner-organisation representatives.

Concept Convergence is supported because the engagement produced the configuration that became the concept design: the standards-derived information architecture, the specified MVP boundary, the concept surfaces and the revised design specification.

Iterative System Building is not claimable because nothing was built. Organizational Integration is not claimable because there was no development-ready design system, reasoning documentation, implementation handover or handover into the client's organisation. Implementation Partnership is not claimable because no implementation support took place.
